PCR, or polymerase chain reaction. It's a laboratory method for exponentially amplifying specific DNA sequences by repeatedly cycling through temperatures that denature, anneal, and extend DNA strands. Invented by Kary Mullis in nineteen eighty-three, it became the cornerstone of modern molecular biology, enabling forensic analysis, gene discovery, viral detection, and clinical diagnostics. Each cycle doubles the target DNA. Around thirty cycles produce a millionfold increase in the amount of DNA. Each cycle has three steps. At high temperature, around ninety-four degrees Celsius, the double helix denatures. At a lower temperature, around fifty degrees Celsius, primers—short DNA probes—bind flanking the target region. At a moderate temperature, around seventy-two degrees Celsius, DNA polymerase extends the primers along the template. The enzyme used, called Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus, is thermostable and survives repeated heating, unlike natural polymerases. Primers define the boundaries of the reaction—they are complementary oligonucleotides that specify exactly which region gets copied. Wrong primers amplify the wrong fragment. Real-time PCR monitors amplification by fluorescence during each cycle, also called quantitative PCR or qPCR. This measures how much product accumulates without waiting until the very end. PCR is used in COVID-nineteen testing, pathogen detection, forensics, cloning, and sequencing library preparation. This technique connects to DNA as the substrate being amplified, DNA polymerase as the enzyme engine and the workhorse of the reaction, gel electrophoresis as the downstream step to confirm PCR product size and purity, molecular cloning where PCR is often the first step to generate fragments for insertion into vectors, DNA sequencing where PCR libraries are prepped by amplifying genomic regions before sequencing, and primers as the short synthetic DNA probes that mark the amplification boundaries.
